notes.A: Dysarthria is impaired motor articulation of speech, generally with language comprehension relatively intact, rather than the receptive language deficit described.
notes.B: Apraxia impairs execution of learned purposeful actions and does not specifically explain difficulty understanding meaningful spoken language.
notes.C: Agnosia refers broadly to impaired recognition despite preserved basic sensation; acquired language comprehension impairment is more specifically classified as receptive aphasia.
notes.E: Broca-type aphasia primarily produces nonfluent, effortful speech with relatively better comprehension of simple language, contrasting with the classical Wernicke pattern.

questions.stem: The relay station through which all sensory input except smell passes on its way to the cortex is the
questions.why: Most sensory pathways relay through specialised thalamic nuclei before reaching primary sensory cortex. Olfaction is the classical exception because initial projections reach primary olfactory cortical regions without an obligatory preceding thalamic relay, although later olfactory processing involves thalamic connections.

notes.A: The hypothalamus integrates autonomic, endocrine and homeostatic information, rather than serving as the principal relay for most conscious sensory pathways to cortex.
notes.B: Basal ganglia participate in motor, cognitive and motivational circuits rather than providing the main ascending sensory relay to primary cortex.
notes.C: The cerebellum integrates sensory feedback for motor coordination but does not constitute the general obligatory relay for sensory information reaching cerebral cortex.
notes.D: The medulla contains important sensory relays and autonomic integration centres, but most major sensory cortical pathways pass through thalamic nuclei.

questions.stem: Homeostatic control of temperature, hunger, thirst and circadian rhythm is centred in the
questions.why: The hypothalamus integrates neural and circulating information to coordinate autonomic, endocrine and behavioural homeostasis. Different hypothalamic regions regulate temperature, feeding, thirst, water balance and circadian timing, including the suprachiasmatic nucleus as a principal circadian pacemaker.

notes.B: The thalamus principally relays and modulates information reaching cortex and participates in arousal, rather than coordinating the listed major homeostatic behaviours.
notes.C: The cerebellum contributes to coordination, timing and motor learning, rather than being the principal regulator of hunger, thirst and body temperature.
notes.D: The pons contains respiratory, arousal and other brainstem circuits, but the central integration of these homeostatic functions occurs chiefly in the hypothalamus.
notes.E: The occipital lobe primarily processes visual information and is not the major central coordinator of endocrine and autonomic homeostatic responses.

questions.stem: The limbic structure essential for forming new long-term (declarative) memories is the
questions.why: The hippocampus and associated medial temporal structures are essential for encoding and consolidating many new declarative memories. Bilateral hippocampal damage can cause severe anterograde amnesia while leaving some older memories, working memory and forms of procedural learning relatively preserved.

notes.A: The cingulate gyrus participates in limbic processing and memory-related networks, but the hippocampus is particularly essential for new declarative memory consolidation.
notes.C: The amygdala assigns emotional significance to experiences and modulates emotional memory, rather than serving as the principal general declarative memory consolidation structure.
notes.D: Certain thalamic nuclei participate in memory circuitry and their lesions can cause amnesia, but the hippocampus is the specified medial temporal structure.
notes.E: The globus pallidus participates in basal ganglia motor and associative circuits, rather than the principal encoding of new declarative memories.

questions.stem: Bilateral destruction of the limbic/amygdaloid region can produce

options.label: A
options.text: loss of pain and temperature sensation

options.label: C
options.text: loss of fear and anger with raised appetite

questions.why: Bilateral damage involving amygdaloid and adjacent anterior temporal limbic structures can produce features of Klüver–Bucy syndrome, including diminished fear responses, behavioural disinhibition and hyperorality or altered eating behaviour. The precise manifestations depend on lesion extent.

notes.A: Pain and temperature loss is associated with damage to somatosensory pathways, rather than the characteristic emotional and behavioural changes following bilateral limbic injury.
notes.B: Resting tremor and rigidity suggest nigrostriatal motor dysfunction, rather than the altered emotional and feeding responses associated with amygdaloid-region damage.
notes.D: Spastic limb paralysis suggests injury to upper motor neuron pathways, not the typical behavioural syndrome following bilateral anterior temporal limbic lesions.
notes.E: Intention tremor and ataxia reflect cerebellar or related pathway dysfunction, rather than the classical changes in emotional reactivity and oral behaviour.

questions.stem: The medulla oblongata contains vital centres for
questions.why: Medullary networks regulate essential autonomic and motor functions, including cardiovascular reflexes, automatic respiratory rhythm and coordination of swallowing. They integrate visceral sensory input and generate outputs through cranial motor nuclei, autonomic pathways and descending spinal connections.

notes.A: Fine voluntary hand movements depend especially on cerebral motor cortex and corticospinal pathways, rather than being primarily organised by medullary autonomic centres.
notes.B: Long-term declarative memory depends substantially on medial temporal and distributed cortical networks, rather than the medulla's vital autonomic control circuits.
notes.C: Colour perception relies on retinal and cerebral visual processing, including specialised occipital and occipitotemporal regions, rather than medullary autonomic centres.
notes.E: Vision and hearing involve retinal and auditory pathways with important midbrain and thalamocortical processing, rather than defining the medulla's major vital control functions.

questions.stem: The sleep-wake cycle and level of consciousness depend on the reticular activating system, concentrated in the
questions.why: Ascending arousal systems include neurons within brainstem reticular formation and associated pontine, midbrain, hypothalamic and basal forebrain networks. Their projections help maintain wakefulness and cortical responsiveness, while interactions with sleep-promoting circuits regulate transitions between sleep and waking.

notes.A: Occipital cortex primarily processes vision, although cortical activation changes with arousal; it is not the main brainstem origin of ascending arousal systems.
notes.B: The cerebellar vermis contributes principally to postural and axial motor coordination, rather than housing the reticular activating system.
notes.C: Dorsal columns carry ascending discriminative touch and proprioceptive information, rather than forming the major distributed neural system maintaining wakefulness.
notes.D: Basal ganglia participate in motor and behavioural regulation, but the classic ascending reticular activating system originates in brainstem reticular networks.

questions.stem: The resting EEG rhythm seen in a relaxed adult with eyes closed is the
questions.why: Alpha activity is a rhythmic EEG pattern, usually approximately 8–13 Hz, prominent over posterior scalp regions during relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed. It typically diminishes with eye opening, visual attention or increased mental engagement.

notes.B: Beta activity has a higher frequency and is commonly associated with alertness, active mental processing or certain medication effects, rather than posterior eyes-closed resting alpha.
notes.C: Delta activity consists of slow waves prominent during deep non-REM sleep, rather than the characteristic rhythm of relaxed awake adults with closed eyes.
notes.D: Theta activity may increase during drowsiness and lighter sleep, rather than being the classic dominant posterior rhythm of relaxed eyes-closed wakefulness.
notes.E: Gamma activity occurs at higher frequencies and participates in several aspects of cortical processing, rather than defining the conventional relaxed resting EEG rhythm.

questions.stem: Rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep is characterised by

options.label: B
options.text: vivid dreaming with a fast, awake-like EEG

questions.why: REM sleep typically shows low-amplitude, mixed-frequency EEG activity resembling wakefulness, rapid eye movements and markedly reduced skeletal muscle tone. Vivid dreams are common, although dreaming can also occur in non-REM sleep.

notes.A: Sleepwalking and night terrors are typically non-REM parasomnias associated particularly with deep slow-wave sleep, rather than defining ordinary REM sleep.
notes.C: The deepest slow-wave sleep corresponds to non-REM stage N3, whereas REM sleep has a relatively activated cortical EEG pattern.
notes.D: High-amplitude delta activity is characteristic of deep non-REM sleep, rather than the usual low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG during REM.
notes.E: The brain remains metabolically and electrically active during REM sleep, despite marked reduction of tone in most skeletal muscles.

questions.stem: The midbrain contains reflex centres mainly for
questions.why: The superior and inferior colliculi of the midbrain participate in visual orienting and auditory processing or reflexive responses, respectively. These tectal structures integrate sensory information with motor circuits that help orient the eyes and head towards relevant stimuli.

notes.A: Speech production involves dominant frontal language and distributed motor networks, rather than the principal visual and auditory reflex centres in the midbrain.
notes.B: Thermoregulatory set-point control depends predominantly on hypothalamic circuits, rather than the tectal sensory orienting structures of the midbrain.
notes.D: Cardiovascular reflex integration occurs chiefly in medullary networks, rather than being the characteristic function of midbrain collicular centres.
notes.E: Declarative memory formation relies particularly on hippocampal and associated cortical circuitry, rather than the midbrain's primary visual and auditory reflex functions.

questions.stem: The tentorium, which separates the hindbrain and brainstem from the rest of the brain, is part of the
questions.why: The tentorium cerebelli is a fold of the meninges; 'infratentorial' means in the hindbrain or brainstem.

questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid is contained within and circulates through the
questions.why: Cerebrospinal fluid occupies the cerebral ventricular system and circulates through interconnected ventricles into the subarachnoid space surrounding brain and spinal cord. It provides mechanical support and contributes to the extracellular environment and clearance of central nervous system substances.

notes.A: Basal ganglia nuclei are collections of neural tissue involved in motor and other functions, rather than CSF-filled cavities forming its major circulation pathways.
notes.B: White-matter tracts consist principally of neural axons and glial cells, rather than the interconnected fluid-filled spaces carrying cerebrospinal fluid.
notes.C: The corpus callosum is a major interhemispheric commissural fibre bundle, rather than part of the ventricular pathway containing cerebrospinal fluid.
notes.D: Dorsal root ganglia house peripheral primary sensory neuron cell bodies, rather than forming the central ventricular spaces through which cerebrospinal fluid circulates.

questions.stem: A fever is produced when pyrogens act on the hypothalamus to
questions.why: Pyrogenic inflammatory signals can increase prostaglandin E2 production and alter hypothalamic thermoregulatory signalling, effectively raising the defended temperature. The body then promotes heat conservation and production until its temperature approaches the higher target, producing fever.

notes.B: Lowering the defended temperature would favour heat loss and oppose fever development, as occurs when the febrile thermoregulatory signal subsides.
notes.C: Fever involves regulated defence of an elevated temperature rather than complete abolition of the body's thermoregulatory target and feedback mechanisms.
notes.D: Cutaneous vasoconstriction helps conserve heat during the rising phase of fever, rather than being permanently blocked by the pyrogen-induced response.
notes.E: Sweating may decrease while temperature rises towards the elevated target and increase when fever resolves; permanent suppression is not required.

questions.stem: In a newborn, non-shivering thermogenesis generates heat mainly in
questions.why: Brown adipose tissue contains abundant mitochondria expressing uncoupling protein 1, which allows proton movement across the inner mitochondrial membrane without equivalent ATP synthesis. Sympathetic activation promotes this heat-producing pathway, particularly important for non-shivering thermogenesis in newborns.

notes.A: The lungs exchange respiratory gases and lose heat through ventilation, rather than being the principal specialised tissue for neonatal non-shivering thermogenesis.
notes.C: Skeletal muscle generates heat through contraction and shivering, but brown adipose tissue is the classic specialised neonatal non-shivering heat source.
notes.D: The liver contributes to basal metabolic heat production, but neonatal adaptive non-shivering thermogenesis relies importantly on uncoupling within brown adipose tissue.
notes.E: The skin regulates heat exchange with the environment, whereas specialised brown adipocytes generate heat through mitochondrial uncoupling rather than primarily cutaneous mechanisms.
